## Series Overview

[Agentic Developer: Zero to Advanced](../agentic-zero-to-advanced/index.qmd) builds its whole
agent architecture around one use case: X-ray defect detection. This short companion series asks
the obvious follow-up question -- is any of that actually specific to X-ray images, or is it just
a reusable shape? To find out, the identical planning/tool-use/reasoning pattern gets rebuilt
around a completely different domain: supply chain.

**The business case:** late or failed deliveries and demand mismatches cost real money, through
expedited shipping, stockouts, or excess inventory. Today a human analyst has to notice something
is off and manually dig through order and shipment data to find the cause. An agent can do that
investigation automatically: it watches incoming orders and shipments, flags anomalies (unusual
delay patterns, a demand spike that doesn't match forecast), reasons over possible causes
(supplier issue, regional disruption, data error), and either recommends an action or drafts an
explanation for a human to review -- turning a reactive, manual investigation process into a
proactive one.

**Dataset:** the DataCo SMART Supply Chain dataset (Mendeley) -- order, shipment, customer, and
product data suitable for a demand/delivery anomaly investigation agent. (Alternative considered:
the SupplyGraph benchmark, graph-structured supply chain planning data from an FMCG company.)

This is a roadmap post: links go live as each part is written, in order.

### Posts in this Series

1. Architecture recap -- same graph, same agent loop shape as the X-ray series, explained briefly
   for readers coming in fresh on this series
2. Swapping in the supply chain scenario -- a demand/delivery anomaly investigation agent built
   with the identical planning and tool-calling pattern, using the DataCo dataset
3. What stayed the same vs. what changed -- defect catalog vs. supplier docs, defect severity vs.
   stockout risk; reflection on architecture portability across domains
